This is not exactly correct - more fair to say South Africa is currently the largest miner of platinum. There are reserves of platinum all around the planet that are not mined. You hear similar claims about rare earth minerals, which the Chinese currently dominate - but only because we closed our own rare earth mines down - due to lack of demand. Most rare earths are not actually rare. Neither are diamonds. Platinum is actually rare like gold is rare, but it is also everywhere like gold too.

As a side note - more than half of most of the rare minerals produced in mining operations are as a byproduct of mining a completely different mineral. For example, the Sudbury nickle mine also produces some small quantities of gold, etc. This happens because the full range of metals tend to be found together in the same deposits, but in different quantities. If the majority product is gold, then you have a gold mine, like that. You're still getting platinum, silver, etc as byproducts, often in quantities too small to economically harvest.

So what this really means is nobody has a correct estimate on what the actual reserves are. Furthermore, nobody can predict how much will be mined in any given season. If the price of nickle goes down, and Sudbury then mines less nickle, they are also mining less gold. Industry wide this has a huge effect when at times half of all silver being produced is a byproduct of other mining operations.

If South Africa goes offline, the price of platinum will surely spike, which then makes it more economical for other mines to look more closely at the platinum side of their own operations, in some cases investment is then made to start harvesting what was previously ignored, and local platinum reserves then "go up."
